subject: maths

moments.title: Two thousand years of failed proof
moments.who: Multiple — Ptolemy, Proclus, Wallis, Saccheri, Lambert, Legendre
moments.body:
Euclid's fifth postulate (the parallel postulate) is messier than the others and seems like it ought to follow from them.

For 2000 years, mathematicians try to prove it. Saccheri (1733) proves it would be equivalent to assuming triangles' angles sum to 180°. He assumes the postulate is FALSE and works out consequences — finding strange but logically consistent geometry. He calls his results 'repugnant to the nature of straight lines' and rejects them. He had non-Euclidean geometry in front of him and didn't see it.
moments.takeaway: The parallel postulate resists every proof. Saccheri stumbles into non-Euclidean geometry but rejects it as obviously wrong.

moments.title: Gauss, Bolyai, Lobachevsky — non-Euclidean geometry
moments.who: Carl Friedrich Gauss (Göttingen), Janos Bolyai (Transylvania), Nikolai Lobachevsky (Kazan)
moments.body:
All three, independently, in the 1820s-30s, realise that the parallel postulate cannot be proved because it's INDEPENDENT. You can replace it with another postulate and get a consistent geometry.

Gauss had worked it out by 1816 but did not publish — he feared 'the clamor of the Boeotians'.

Lobachevsky publishes in 1829 in an obscure Russian journal. He is mostly ignored, occasionally ridiculed. He dies in 1856, his reputation only beginning to recover.

Bolyai's father Wolfgang sends his son's 1832 manuscript to Gauss, who replies that he had worked out the same results himself decades earlier. Bolyai is crushed. He stops publishing mathematics.

quote.text: Out of nothing I have created a strange new universe.

moments.takeaway: Non-Euclidean geometry is discovered independently three times. Two of the discoverers are destroyed by Gauss's claim of priority.

moments.title: Riemann's habilitation lecture
moments.body:
Bernhard Riemann, defending his habilitation, gives a lecture 'On the Hypotheses which lie at the Foundations of Geometry'. He generalises non-Euclidean geometry to ANY number of dimensions and to spaces with arbitrary 'curvature' varying from point to point.

The lecture is so far ahead of its time that the only audience member who fully understands is Gauss — who is so impressed he praises Riemann publicly (unusual for Gauss).

Riemann's framework includes Euclidean and the standard non-Euclidean geometries as special cases. He proposes that the geometry of physical space might be measured experimentally.
moments.takeaway: Riemann generalises geometry beyond surfaces to manifolds of any dimension. The mathematical language for general relativity exists 60 years before it's needed.

moments.title: Beltrami's model
moments.body:
Beltrami publishes a model of non-Euclidean (hyperbolic) geometry inside Euclidean space. He shows that hyperbolic geometry can be realised as the geometry of points on a pseudosphere (a surface of constant negative curvature).

The model proves that hyperbolic geometry is consistent if Euclidean geometry is. Non-Euclidean geometry is no longer a theoretical curiosity — it's geometrically and physically meaningful.
moments.takeaway: Non-Euclidean geometry is consistent. It cannot be 'disproved' by appeal to Euclidean intuitions because it exists INSIDE Euclidean space, on curved surfaces.

moments.title: General relativity
moments.who: Albert Einstein and Marcel Grossmann, Berlin
moments.body:
Einstein, working with Marcel Grossmann (his old college friend, by then a mathematician), uses Riemannian geometry to describe gravity. Spacetime curvature replaces gravitational force. The Schwarzschild solution (1916) for a spherically symmetric mass gives a non-Euclidean geometry around stars and planets.

The Eddington solar eclipse expedition (1919) confirms light bending around the sun. Riemann's pure mathematics turns out to describe physical reality.
moments.takeaway: Pure mathematics, developed for its own sake over a century, becomes the foundation of fundamental physics.

now.title: Non-Euclidean geometry today
now.body:
Riemannian geometry is standard in physics (general relativity, gauge theories), differential geometry, geometric topology, and machine learning (manifold learning, hyperbolic embeddings).

Applications include GPS (which requires general relativistic corrections), cosmology (the geometry of the universe), computer graphics, robotics, and the study of complex networks.
now.open_questions: What is the actual geometry of the universe (spatially flat to within current measurement precision, but is it finite or infinite)? How can we develop intuition for higher-dimensional curved spaces? Are there entirely new geometric structures we haven't yet conceived?

reflection: Bolyai and Lobachevsky both died ignored. Gauss didn't publish for fear of controversy. Riemann's deepest insights were not appreciated for half a century. Einstein needed all their work — and the mathematician (Grossmann) who could translate it — to formulate general relativity. What if non-Euclidean geometry had never been pursued? Could 20th-century physics have happened?
